Apply now Course Details DURATION 20 WEEKS FORMAT PEER-LED LEARNING START DATE December 2, 2026 COST FREE How Our Courses Work Our courses are built on a peer-teaching approach to ensure a thorough understanding of the material. 1 Expert Input An industry expert introduces the topic through a live lecture. 2 Become a Specialist In teams of three , you research a subtopic and prepare a 10–15-minute presentation. 3 Teach your Peers The following week, you present your findings to other groups and learn from their subtopics. 4 Build on What You Learn The next lecture week introduces a new topic. Repeat this cycle across 10 topics in 20 weeks. Previous speakers Speakers from previous cohorts. The upcoming cohort’s lineup will be announced separately. Dr. David An Partner @Dracoon Ventures Previous topic: "Proof of Work, Mining, and Immutability" Jonas Gebele Research Associate @Technical University of Munich Previous topic: "Cryptography and Hashing" David Kurz Business Development @Bitvavo Previous topic: "Ethereum: The World Computer (Architecture)" What to expect Certification Eligible participants receive a PDF and NFT certificate after completing the cohort. Detailed eligibility criteria will be confirmed before the program begins. Speakers Expert-led lectures introduce each topic, with time for questions and discussion. Learning format Expert lectures, small-group research, and peer teaching help you build a thorough understanding of each topic. Projects Project opportunities and requirements will be shared once confirmed. You don’t just get a course. You get a community . Web3 Talents welcomes everyone, whether you’ve never heard of blockchain or you’re already working in the space as a seasoned professional, our teaching platform ensures you’ll always have something to contribute and something new to discover. “I joined the course with almost no prior knowledge of Web3, but the structure made it easy to follow. The sessions were beginner-friendly, and the community helped me feel more confident asking questions and exploring the topic further.” Anna Course participant “I liked that the course didn't assume everyone already knew the terminology. It started with the basics and then slowly connected the topics, which made the more technical parts easier to understand.” Anoushk Course participant “The group research format was useful because it made me go deeper into one topic instead of only listening passively. Presenting it to others also helped me understand where I still had gaps.” Adam Course participant “The diversity of the cohort. There was a lot to learn from everyone.” Anonymous Course participant Find out more Check out TUM Blockchain Learn. Connect. Explore Web3. courses.text: Skip to content Home Courses Community Apply now Start date: December 2, 2026 Blockchain Fundamentals 1 Free · 20 weeks Blockchain Fundamentals 1 is a free, 20-week program combining expert lectures, small-group research, and peer teaching across 10 topics. Join us online on Wednesdays at 6 PM Berlin time, starting December 2, 2026. Application deadline: November 8, 2026 at 23:59. Acceptance announcements: November 22, 2026. Apply now Course information From digital trust and Bitcoin to smart contracts, DeFi, and crypto taxation: build your understanding one topic at a time. Course Description Curriculum FAQ How you’ll learn Lecture weeks and presentation weeks alternate. An industry expert introduces a topic in a live lecture with Q&A. In small peer groups of three, you research one of four subtopics and prepare a 10–15-minute presentation. The following week, you teach your subtopic to other groups and learn from theirs — the jigsaw learning model. A new topic begins at the next lecture session. Sessions & participation Sessions last 1.5 hours and take place online on Wednesdays at 6 PM Berlin time. Teams rotate during the program so you can work with more peers. Use Moodle for materials and assignments, and Zoom for meetings; recordings and additional learning resources are provided. Cameras are required during sessions. Preparing your presentations For each presentation, create an original diagram, timeline, or comparison table, and use primary sources such as whitepapers and developer documentation. Set aside additional time outside sessions for research and preparation. One topic. Two weeks. Wednesdays at 6 PM Berlin time · 1.5-hour online sessions. Research and preparation happen between the two sessions. Week 1 Learn & prepare Expert lecture An industry expert introduces the topic in a live lecture with Q&A. Research & prepare After the lecture, work in a team of three to research one of four subtopics. Prepare a 10–15-minute presentation with an original diagram, timeline, or comparison table, using primary sources. Between sessions — not a separate week. Week 2 Present & exchange Peer teaching Present your subtopic to other groups and learn from theirs. Together, piece together the full topic through the jigsaw learning model. The following week, a new expert lecture begins the next topic. Repeat with the next topic · 10 topics over 20 weeks. Each topic builds on the ones before it. Lectures connect back to concepts from earlier weeks, so you can recall them, and point ahead to what is still to come. Expand All Phase 1: Foundational Trust · Weeks 1–4 The goal here is to establish the need for blockchain by conceptually solving the double-spending problem, then introducing the mathematical concepts that make it possible. Topic 1 Weeks 1–2: The Need for Decentralization & Digital Trust Centralized vs. Decentralized Systems: An introduction to centralized and decentralized systems. The problems of centralized systems and the advantages of decentralization. The Double-Spending Problem: Why digital money needs a trusted party, and what breaks without one. The Shared Ledger: An introduction to the concept of a shared, immutable ledger, with a basic overview of public vs. private ledgers. Topic 2 Weeks 3–4: Cryptography: Hashing, Keys & Signatures Part A (Integrity): Hashing, mathematical trust and one-way functions. How these primitives build the foundation of trust, and how they connect to the bigger picture of blockchain and to Topic 1. Hands-on: see a hash function in action. Change the input and watch how the output changes. Part B (Identity): Basic cryptographic principles (symmetric vs. asymmetric). How public/private key pairs work, and how digital signatures are used for authorization. Explained intuitively, with everyday examples, so no technical background is needed. Phase 2: The Ledger Architecture · Weeks 5–8 This phase builds the identity layer and then the data layer of the first major blockchain implementation: Bitcoin. Topic 3 Weeks 5–6: Wallets, Peer-to-Peer Networks & Propagation Wallets: Wallet types (hot/cold, custodial/non-custodial) and key management best practices (MultiSig). The Network: Decentralized network communication and node roles (full, light, archival). Propagation: Gossip protocols, and how data such as transactions and blocks propagates across the network. Topic 4 Weeks 7–8: Bitcoin: Data Structure & Transactions Block Structure: The structure of a Bitcoin block: header and transactions. Transaction Flow: Creation, signing, the mempool, and confirmation. UTXO Model: How the unspent transaction output model works. Phase 3: Securing the State · Weeks 9–12 This phase focuses on the mechanisms used to agree on the single, correct history of transactions, and then on what that agreed state can hold once the ledger becomes programmable. Topic 5 Weeks 9–10: Proof-of-Work, Proof-of-Stake & the Blockchain Trilemma Recap: Why immutability required a costly puzzle, bridging from Topic 4’s UTXO model and block structure. PoW Core Loop: Hash-below-target, the nonce, halving, and why scarcity is engineered. The 51% Attack: An economic argument, not just a technical one. PoS as an Alternative: Bonding capital instead of burning energy, the validator lifecycle, and slashing as the “cost of cheating”. The Blockchain Trilemma: The unifying lens: PoW, PoS, DPoS (TRON/EOS) and BFT (Cosmos) plotted on the same triangle. Topic 6 Weeks 11–12: Architectural Shift: The “World Computer” (Ethereum) The Transition: From a single-purpose ledger to a general-purpose blockchain. State Machine: Moving from “Who has money?” (Bitcoin) to “What is the state of this application?” (Ethereum), and the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) as a shared, singleton state machine. Account Model: Why Ethereum uses accounts (like a bank) instead of UTXOs for programmability. EVM Intro: The global computer that everyone runs simultaneously. Phase 4: The Programmable Layer · Weeks 13–16 This phase covers what runs on top of the world computer, smart contracts and tokens, and how to judge the economics of those tokens. Topic 7 Weeks 13–14: Smart Contracts, Gas, Token Standards & Oracles Smart Contracts: The concept of “Code is Law”. The Fuel (Gas): Why computation costs money (protection against the Halting Problem), and gas limit vs. gas price. Token Standards (The Primitives): The building blocks for assets on Ethereum: ERC-20 (Fungible): Creating “currency” or “shares” on top of Ethereum. ERC-721 (Non-Fungible/NFT): Unique identifiers for digital art, certificates, or identity. Oracles: The “walled garden” problem, and how blockchains access off-chain data (e.g. Chainlink) to trigger contracts. Topic 8 Weeks 15–16: Tokenomics Why Tokenomics Matters: Tokens have no agreed valuation standard like equity. The market built its own metrics instead, and this lecture teaches how to read them. Market Cap: Price × circulating supply: what the market currently values the tradeable tokens at. FDV (Fully Diluted Valuation): Price × max supply: the valuation if every token that will ever exist were already circulating. The Gap Between Them (Low Float Trap): A big MC/FDV gap means most of the supply hasn’t hit the market yet, so dilution is coming. NVT Ratio: Network Value to Transactions. Like a P/E ratio, it compares market cap to actual on-chain usage. Connecting the Dots: Links back to Topic 7’s token standards (supply parameters live in the contract) and Topic 5’s staking (staked supply shrinks the effective float). Phase 5: The New Economy · Weeks 17–20 Applying the programmable layer to finance (DeFi), and the rules that come with it. Topic 9 Weeks 17–18: The Financial Layer: Stablecoins, Real World Assets & DeFi Intro Stablecoins: The bridge between fiat and crypto. Types: Fiat-backed (USDC/Tether) vs. crypto-backed (DAI) vs. algorithmic. The Stablecoin Trilemma: Stability, capital efficiency, and decentralization. Real World Assets (RWA): Tokenizing off-chain assets such as real estate, T-bills, and gold, and the legal and technical challenges of enforcing on-chain ownership of off-chain assets. DeFi Intro: Finance without intermediaries: DEX (Decentralized Exchange): Automated Market Makers (AMM) vs. order books, and how Uniswap works without a middleman. Lending/Borrowing: Over-collateralized loans (Aave/Compound): “Be your own bank.” Topic 10 Weeks 19–20: Taxation in Crypto The Shift: Crypto’s “nobody’s watching” era is ending. Learn which actions trigger tax. Regulation: MiCA (the EU-wide license) and DAC8 (the EU version of CARF), which has collected transaction data since January 1, 2026, with the first cross-border exchange between tax authorities in 2027. One Investor’s Year: Buy, swap into DeFi, stake, sell: every tax trigger is flagged live on Blockpit’s tracker. Germany Basics: Crypto as a private asset (§23 EStG), the one-year holding period (Spekulationsfrist), and the €1,000 Freigrenze. Connecting the Dots: Staking rewards are taxed differently than the underlying asset, and swaps and LP moves in DeFi each carry their own tax event. Who can join? Eligibility and prerequisites will be confirmed with the course details. How much time is required? The free, 20-week program starts on December 2, 2026. Join a 1.5-hour online session on Wednesdays at 6 PM Berlin time, alternating lecture and presentation weeks. Allow additional time for group research and preparation; that workload is not yet specified. How do I apply? Apply through the application form . Applications run from October 12 to November 8, 2026 at 23:59. Acceptance announcements: November 22, 2026. The deadline timezone is still to be confirmed. What time are the sessions? Sessions take place on Wednesdays at 6 PM Berlin time and last 1.5 hours. The first session is December 2, 2026. Holiday-break dates and the final calendar will be shared separately. Will I receive a certificate? Eligible participants receive a PDF and NFT certificate after the cohort. Detailed participation and points requirements will be confirmed before the program begins. Previous speakers Speakers from previous cohorts. The upcoming cohort’s lineup will be announced separately. Dr. David An Partner @Dracoon Ventures Previous topic: "Proof of Work, Mining, and Immutability" Jonas Gebele Research Associate @Technical University of Munich Previous topic: "Cryptography and Hashing" David Kurz Business Development @Bitvavo Previous topic: "Ethereum: The World Computer (Architecture)" Hear From the Students “I joined the course with almost no prior knowledge of Web3, but the structure made it easy to follow. The sessions were beginner-friendly, and the community helped me feel more confident asking questions and exploring the topic further.” Anna Course participant “I liked that the course didn't assume everyone already knew the terminology. It started with the basics and then slowly connected the topics, which made the more technical parts easier to understand.” Anoushk Course participant “The group research format was useful because it made me go deeper into one topic instead of only listening passively. Presenting it to others also helped me understand where I still had gaps.” Adam Course participant “The diversity of the cohort. There was a lot to learn from everyone.” Anonymous Course participant Learn. Connect. Explore Web3. community.text: Skip to content Home Courses Community Apply now Get to know our Community Join Our Vibrant Web3 Community Web3Talents is a community where students learn, connect, and grow together. Members share ideas, support each other, and explore the world of Web3. Together with groups like the TUM Blockchain Club, we make blockchain learning fun and accessible. Built by students, driven by vision. Diversity is Key We believe that everyone has a place in Web3, and the best growth happens when we learn from our collective differences. Students Eager to specialize in blockchain and Web3 technologies Industry Professionals Eager to specialize in blockchain and Web3 technologies Interested Minds Eager to specialize in blockchain and Web3 technologies Community events CONFERENCE October 29–31, 2026 TUM Blockchain Conference House of Communication, Munich More Info Community event updates Event announcements Confirmed community events will be announced here. Session details Topics, hosts, and formats will be listed once confirmed. Locations Event locations or online joining details will be shared when available. Participation Registration and eligibility details will accompany each confirmed event. Any Questions? Is the program free? Yes. Blockchain Fundamentals 1 is free to join. How can we apply to the courses? Apply through the application form . Applications run from October 12 to November 8, 2026 at 23:59. Acceptance announcements: November 22, 2026. The deadline timezone is still to be confirmed. How time consuming is each course program? The free, 20-week program starts on December 2, 2026. Join a 1.5-hour online session on Wednesdays at 6 PM Berlin time, alternating lecture and presentation weeks. Allow additional time for group research and preparation; that workload is not yet specified. Can I still join the events even if I'm not a member? Participation requirements will be included with each confirmed event. Learn. Connect. Explore Web3.
